texts.label: A
texts.title: The manager
texts.text: Silence in a meeting is not necessarily agreement. Some colleagues need time to test an idea before speaking, while others may feel that the room has already decided. I now leave a deliberate pause and invite views individually rather than rewarding the fastest voice.

texts.label: B
texts.title: The designer
texts.text: My best design decisions rarely arrive during discussion. They emerge afterwards, when fragments of other people’s comments have had time to combine. I regard silence as part of the creative process, not as evidence that the meeting failed.

texts.label: The mediator
texts.title: The mediator
texts.text: Silence can be an active intervention. When two people are arguing, a pause may stop them repeating positions and create room for a different question. It is useful only if the mediator can tolerate the discomfort it produces.

texts.label: D
texts.title: The consultant
texts.text: I am cautious about celebrating silence. In some organisations, it reflects a hierarchy in which disagreement carries a career cost. Asking people to speak more is not enough; leaders must show that dissent has consequences they can accept.

questions.prompt: Who sees silence as something that can hide unequal participation?
questions.explanation: The manager notes that quiet colleagues may feel the room has already decided.

questions.prompt: Who describes a delay as helpful to creative thinking?
questions.explanation: The designer says ideas emerge after comments have had time to combine.

questions.prompt: Who uses silence to interrupt a repetitive dispute?
questions.explanation: The mediator presents a pause as a way to stop repeated positions.

questions.prompt: Who argues that organisational power can make speaking risky?
questions.explanation: The consultant connects silence with hierarchy and the cost of disagreement.
